steps.body: Subtraction runs the same course: rename to a shared size, then take one count from the other.
steps.narration: Subtraction runs the same course: rename to a shared size, then take one count from the other.

widget.prompt: Subtract 4/12 from 9/12 and build what is left.
widget.successFeedback: 5/12 — nine twelfths with four removed, still measured in twelfths.
widget.lowFeedback: That build is SHORTER than 5/12 — either shade more pieces or make each piece larger until the lengths match.
widget.highFeedback: That build is LONGER than 5/12 — either shade fewer pieces or make each piece smaller until the lengths match.

commonFractions.feedback: Sixths are twice the size of twelfths; removing twelfths leaves twelfths behind.
12/12 is one whole — adding instead of removing overshoots what is actually left.

predict.reveal: Halves and thirds are different sizes, so there is nothing to take away until both are sixths.

cml.actionGoal: Rename both fractions to the same piece size, then count the pieces for g5u sub.
invariants: Fractions add and subtract only when their pieces are the same size: renaming scales both parts of a fraction and leaves its value untouched, which is what makes g5u sub a counting problem once the denominators agree.
misconceptions: Adding numerators and denominators across, scaling only one part of a fraction when renaming, or forgetting to trade a whole when the top fraction is too small to subtract from.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If only the numerators were made equal instead of the denominators, what would go wrong?

widget.prompt: Once renamed, 4/6 litre were available and 1/6 litre was poured out. Express what is left as ?/6. What is the numerator?

commonErrors.feedback: That joined the two amounts; pouring out removes pieces rather than adding them.
6 names the piece size, which never changes — only how many are left.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Give both fractions the same piece size first; after that the pieces simply count.

widget.prompt: When you add 6/12 + 5/12, what happens to the denominator?

options.label: It stays 12 because the piece size never changes
options.feedback: Correct — adding counts how many same-size pieces you hold; it never re-cuts them.

options.label: It becomes 24
options.feedback: Doubling the denominator would halve every piece, changing the amount instead of counting it.

options.label: It becomes 11
options.feedback: That is the numerator of the answer — the count of pieces, not their size.

options.label: It disappears
options.feedback: Without a denominator the pieces have no size, and the answer would name nothing.
